name: Mocking Conventions
description: This module defines the naming, formatting, and structural style conventions to follow whenever writing, implementing, or reviewing mocking code or output, so results stay consistent with the existing mocking style guide.
content:
This module defines the naming, formatting, and structural style conventions to follow whenever writing, implementing, or reviewing mocking code or output, so results stay consistent with the existing mocking style guide.

CORE GUIDELINES
1. Keep mocking changes scoped to what was asked; avoid unrelated cleanup in the same pass.
2. Keep mocking outputs reproducible: fix seeds, record versions, and avoid hidden non-determinism where it matters.
3. Before starting mocking work, confirm the scope and constraints so the approach matches the actual requirement.
4. Prefer the simplest mocking approach that satisfies the requirement over a more general one that isn't needed yet.
5. State assumptions about mocking explicitly before proceeding, rather than leaving them implicit.
6. Measure before optimizing any mocking bottleneck; do not guess at what is slow.
7. Document any non-obvious mocking decision with a short rationale so future readers understand the 'why', not just the 'what'.
8. Validate mocking outputs against a concrete example before treating the work as complete.
9. Prefer explicit, readable mocking solutions over clever ones that are hard to verify.
10. Surface known limitations of a chosen mocking approach instead of presenting it as complete when it is not.
11. Check that mocking terminology is used consistently throughout, matching existing conventions in the surrounding context.
12. When multiple mocking strategies are viable, name the trade-off explicitly rather than silently picking one.

COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID
- Avoid introducing new mocking abstractions before there is a second concrete use case that needs them.
- Do not skip documenting mocking assumptions just because they seem obvious in the moment.
- Do not silently drop mocking edge cases to make an example look cleaner than the real system.
- Do not apply generic mocking advice without checking it fits the specific context at hand.
- Do not treat a single passing example as full verification of mocking correctness.

CLOSING NOTE
These guidelines are a starting point for mocking, not an exhaustive rulebook — use judgment when a rule doesn't fit the situation.
